content.title: About
content.content: Baked beans, reduced sodium are canned beans cooked in a savory tomato sauce with less added salt. They retain the classic sweet‑savory flavor while being suitable for those watching their sodium intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Baked beans became popular in the United States in the early 20th century as a quick, hearty meal for workers.
The reduced‑sodium version uses spices and tomato paste to replace much of the salt.
One 425 g package provides about 1.5 g of protein and 5 g of dietary fiber.
Tomato sauce is rich in lycopene, an antioxidant linked to heart health.
Glass jars preserve flavor better than metal cans.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Beans supply a complete set of essential amino acids, beneficial for vegetarians and athletes.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports regular bowel movements and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: Reduced salt helps maintain healthy blood pressure.

items.title: Source of iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals aid in hemoglobin formation and muscle function.

items.title: Lycopene and other antioxidants
items.content: The tomato base provides lycopene, which protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Tomato sauce can contain added sugar; people with diabetes should account for it.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Beans may cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive persons.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain brands may include preservatives such as sodium benzoate.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve baked beans as a side dish, add them to chili, casseroles, salads, or use as a filling for tortillas. They heat quickly in the microwave or on the stovetop.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the unopened jar in a cool, dry place. After opening, store in the refrigerator in an airtight container and consume within 5 days. Discard if you notice off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit punch is a refreshing beverage made from fruit juices mixed with carbonated water. It combines the natural sweetness of fruits with a light fizz, creating a bright flavor suitable for both children and adults.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first fruit punch appeared in the United States in the early 1920s.
Blending different juices (orange, pineapple, cherry) provides a variety of taste notes.
Carbonated water helps quench thirst more quickly.
Punch is often served at parties and summer cafés as a non‑alcoholic alternative.

items.title: Vitamin boost
items.content: Fresh fruit juice is rich in vitamin C and other antioxidants that support the immune system.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Carbonated water contributes to rapid fluid replenishment.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The drink contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Fruit juices provide potassium, magnesium, and small amounts of calcium, beneficial for heart and muscle function.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some versions may contain added sugar, increasing the calorie count.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity of fruit juices can irritate the stomach in people with gastritis.

items.title: Carbonation
items.content: The fizz may cause bloating in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve fruit punch chilled in glasses or cups. Garnish with fruit slices, mint leaves, or ice cubes. It works as a standalone drink or as a base for non‑alcoholic cocktails.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared punch in the refrigerator in a sealed container for no more than 3‑4 days. For longer storage, keep the carbonated water separate from the juice to preserve fizz.

potato-salad-with-egg-made-with-any-type.title: Potato Salad with Egg and Fat‑Free Dressing

content.title: About
content.content: A salad made from boiled potatoes, hard‑boiled eggs and any fat‑free dressing (such as mustard‑vinegar sauce, low‑fat yogurt dressing or a simple vinaigrette). It is a light, diet‑friendly dish rich in protein, B‑vitamins and fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potatoes are one of the world’s most consumed vegetables and provide vitamin C and potassium.
Eggs are a complete source of all essential amino acids.
Fat‑free dressings keep the calorie count low while still delivering flavor through herbs, mustard and vinegar.
The salad is usually served cold, making it ideal for picnics and work lunches.
Different cultures add various herbs: dill in Russia, green onion in the US, and nori in Japan.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Eggs and potatoes together provide high‑quality animal and plant protein that supports tissue repair.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: The absence of fat in the dressing reduces the overall energy density, helpful for weight management.

items.title: Potassium source
items.content: Potatoes supply potassium, which helps maintain fluid balance and normal blood pressure.

items.title: B‑vitamin rich
items.content: Eggs are rich in vitamin B12, while potatoes provide vitamin B6, both important for nervous system function.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from potatoes and added herbs promotes healthy bowel movements.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Adding too much salt to the dressing can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Eggs should be fully cooked to avoid salmonella.

items.title: High glycemic index of potatoes
items.content: People with diabetes should monitor portion size because potatoes raise blood glucose quickly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as a standalone dish, a side to meat or fish, or in sandwiches. Fresh herbs (dill, parsley), green onions or a dash of mustard can enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Add the dressing just before serving to prevent the potatoes from becoming soggy.

content.title: About
content.content: Rice, white, cooked, fat added is boiled white rice to which a plant or animal fat (oil, butter, margarine) has been incorporated during cooking. This product is commonly used to enhance flavor and increase the energy value of dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice loses most of its fiber and micronutrients during milling, but remains a good source of carbohydrates.
Adding fat improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins such as A and D when they are present in the meal.
In many Asian cuisines rice is cooked with oil or coconut milk to make it richer and more satisfying.
Cooking rice with fat reduces stickiness, resulting in more separate grains.
Rice is a staple food for more than half of the world’s population.

items.title: Energy density
items.content: The added fat raises the calorie content, which can be beneficial for individuals with high energy needs.

items.title: Improved satiety and taste
items.content: Fats enhance flavor and promote a longer feeling of fullness.

items.title: Better absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: Presence of fat helps the body absorb vitamins A, D, E and K more efficiently if they are part of the dish.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Rice provides a quick source of glucose, essential for brain and muscle energy.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: Boiled rice is gentle on the digestive system, making it suitable for diets with gastrointestinal concerns.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The added fat significantly increases calories, which may contribute to weight gain if consumed in excess.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Using butter or palm oil can raise saturated fat levels, which is undesirable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice has a high glycemic index and can cause rapid blood sugar spikes, especially in people with diabetes.

items.title: Allergy to added oils
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to certain plant oils.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rice with added fat can be served as a side dish with meat, fish or vegetables, used in pilaf, fried rice, sushi, or as a base for salads. Garnish with fresh herbs, spices or sauces for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked rice in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: The French roll (sometimes called Vienna roll) is a light, airy bread roll made from wheat flour, yeast, milk, butter, and a small amount of sugar. The dough is allowed to rise, creating a characteristic porous crumb, then shaped into small round buns and baked to a golden crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally the French roll is baked in French and Austrian bakeries, where it is served at breakfast or as a snack.
The name "Vienna" arose from the roll's popularity in Viennese cafés in the 19th century.
The dough is often proofed for more than 12 hours, which develops complex aromatic compounds.
In some regions the rolls are sprinkled with coarse sea salt or poppy seeds for extra flavor and texture.
French rolls are frequently used as a base for ham, cheese, and fresh‑vegetable sandwiches.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: The roll provides a quick source of energy thanks to easily digestible carbs.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: The dough supplies B1, B2 and niacin, which support metabolism.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Flour and milk deliver calcium, iron and magnesium.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with baguettes or croissants, the roll contains less saturated fat.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Its soft, porous texture makes it gentle on the digestive system, especially for children and seniors.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The roll contains wheat flour and is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Because of rapid carbohydrate absorption, the roll can raise blood sugar levels, which is important for diabetics to consider.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some versions are salted; those monitoring sodium intake should choose an unsalted option.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the roll fresh, split it and spread butter, jam, or cream cheese. It works well for sandwiches, toasties and appetizers. Warm rolls are often paired with hot chocolate or coffee.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the roll in an airtight bag at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage place it in the refrigerator (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 2 months). Reheat in the oven before serving to restore a crisp crust.

content.title: About
content.content: Diet root beer is a non‑alcoholic carbonated beverage with the characteristic flavor of sassafras root, vanilla, anise and spices. The diet version uses artificial sweeteners instead of sugar, making it low‑calorie.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Root beer originated in North America in the 19th century as a homemade herbal brew.
Traditional flavor is achieved with sassafras root extract, though many modern brands use flavorings.
Diet versions appeared in the 1970s alongside the rise of low‑calorie products.
In the US, root beer is often served over ice in a “flat glass” and sometimes with a scoop of vanilla ice cream (root beer float).
Some brands sweeten their diet root beer with stevia or sucralose.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: Diet root beer contains 0–5 kcal per 100 ml, allowing enjoyment without a significant energy load.

items.title: Sugar‑free
items.content: The absence of sugar makes it suitable for people monitoring blood glucose levels.

items.title: Contains plant extracts
items.content: Sassafras and anise extracts may provide mild antioxidant effects.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Like any carbonated drink, it contributes to fluid intake when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Alcohol‑free
items.content: Appropriate for all ages, including children and pregnant women, provided there are no contraindications to artificial sweeteners.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to sucralose, aspartame or other sweeteners, experiencing gastrointestinal discomfort.

items.title: Carbonation
items.content: Excessive consumption of carbonated drinks can cause bloating and discomfort in people with irritable bowel syndrome.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic pH may contribute to tooth enamel erosion with frequent use.

items.title: Allergy to flavorings
items.content: Rarely, allergic reactions to plant extracts such as sassafras can occur.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Serve chilled, optionally over ice. Commonly used as a base for non‑alcoholic cocktails or in a root beer float with a scoop of vanilla ice cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 7–10 days.

content.title: About
content.content: The liquid sugar substitute NFS (5022) is a zero‑calorie sweetener based on sucralose, designed for use in beverages, baking and cooking. It dissolves completely in water, leaves no aftertaste and is suitable for low‑sugar diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sucralose is about 600 times sweeter than sugar but is not metabolized by the body.
The liquid form allows precise dosing in industrial production.
The product is approved by the FDA and EFSA as safe for consumption.
It does not raise blood glucose levels, making it suitable for diabetics.
Stable at temperatures up to 200 °C, suitable for baking.

items.title: Weight management support
items.content: Zero calories help reduce overall energy intake when replacing sugar.

items.title: Blood sugar stability
items.content: Does not cause glucose spikes, beneficial for pre‑diabetic and diabetic individuals.

items.title: Dental health
items.content: Not fermented by oral bacteria, does not contribute to tooth decay.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rare individual hypersensitivity to sucralose may occur.

items.title: Digestive tolerance
items.content: Large amounts can cause mild gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive people.

items.title: Not recommended for children under 3
items.content: Due to limited data on long‑term effects on development.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add the liquid sweetener to tea, coffee, cocktails, sauces, marinades and dough at 1 % of the weight of sugar being replaced. Stir well to ensure complete dissolution.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a tightly sealed container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Shelf life is 24 months when stored properly.

content.title: About
content.content: A taco is a Mexican dish consisting of a soft or crispy tortilla filled with various ingredients. This version features beans, spices and vegetables, with no cheese added.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional Mexican tacos use corn tortillas, though flour versions are also common.
Beans are the main protein source in vegetarian tacos.
Tacos are often served with salsa, guacamole and lime.
The dish gained worldwide popularity in the 1990s through fast‑food chains.

items.title: Rich plant protein
items.content: Beans provide all essential amino acids, making them a solid meat alternative.

items.title: High fiber content
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low saturated fat
items.content: Omitting cheese reduces saturated fat levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beans are a good source of folate, thiamine and niacin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Polyphenols in beans help combat free radicals.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Beans can cause bloating in sensitive people.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid may reduce mineral absorption; soaking beans is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tacos can be enjoyed on their own or with salsa, guacamole, fresh veggies and a squeeze of lime. Lightly toast the tortilla for extra crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep tortillas in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. Store cooked beans in the refrigerator in a sealed container for no more than 4 days.
